questions.question: Why use VLSM for LANs requiring different host counts?

options.A: Every LAN must receive an identical prefix length
options.B: Each LAN can receive a prefix sized to its needs
options.C: Each LAN avoids reserving a network address
options.D: Each host can share the same address across adjoining LANs

questions.explanation: Varying subnet sizes reduces unused space while preserving separate LAN prefixes.

option_explanations.A: Identical lengths are characteristic of fixed-length subnetting.
option_explanations.B: Varying subnet sizes reduces unused space while preserving separate LAN prefixes.
option_explanations.C: A conventional VLSM LAN still reserves its network address.
option_explanations.D: Overlapping LANs in the same forwarding domain cannot freely share individual addresses.

questions.question: When allocating a fresh block manually, why place the largest requirements first?

options.A: Large blocks have fewer aligned placement choices
options.B: All allocations must use ascending prefix lengths
options.C: Large blocks do not need aligned network IDs
options.D: Small blocks cannot use the remaining gaps

questions.explanation: Larger allocations have stricter alignment and can be harder to place after fragmentation.

option_explanations.A: Larger allocations have stricter alignment and can be harder to place after fragmentation.
option_explanations.B: Largest-first is a placement strategy, not a required ordering of every plan.
option_explanations.C: Every prefix has an alignment boundary.
option_explanations.D: Small blocks generally have more options for fitting into remaining aligned space.

questions.question: What is the smallest conventional LAN subnet that supports 62 usable addresses?
questions.explanation: Six host bits provide 64 addresses and 62 usable slots.

option_explanations.C: A /25 supplies 126 but is larger than necessary.
option_explanations.D: Six host bits provide 64 addresses and 62 usable slots.

questions.question: Why is 192.0.2.48/27 unsuitable as the network ID of a new allocation?

options.B: A /27 requires the final octet to be zero

questions.explanation: A /27 has boundaries every 32 addresses. .48 has nonzero host bits.

option_explanations.A: A /27 has boundaries every 32 addresses. .48 has nonzero host bits.
option_explanations.B: Valid /27 network IDs occur every 32 addresses, including nonzero boundaries.

questions.question: A designer reserves 192.0.2.0/25 and 192.0.2.128/26. Which lowest-address aligned /27 remains available?
questions.explanation: The reserved ranges end at .191. .192 and .224 both fit, with .192 lowest.

option_explanations.A: .176 is unaligned for a /27 and lies in the reserved .128–.191 block.
option_explanations.B: .160 is aligned but lies inside the reserved /26.
option_explanations.C: The reserved ranges end at .191. .192 and .224 both fit, with .192 lowest.

questions.question: Which one route summarizes exactly 172.28.44.0/24 and 172.28.45.0/24?
questions.explanation: The adjacent third octets begin on an even /23 boundary.

option_explanations.A: It includes only the second of the requested /24s.
option_explanations.C: The adjacent third octets begin on an even /23 boundary.
option_explanations.D: This includes third octets 46 and 47 as well.

questions.question: Which prefix covers exactly 198.51.100.0/25, .128/26 and .192/26 in the same /24?
questions.explanation: The two /26 blocks combine into the upper /25. Together the two /25s form the entire /24.

option_explanations.A: The two /26 blocks combine into the upper /25. Together the two /25s form the entire /24.
option_explanations.B: This covers only the upper half of the required space.
option_explanations.D: This covers only the lower half of the requested space.

questions.question: A team needs 120, 60, 28 and 12 usable LAN addresses. How much space remains after allocating smallest suitable subnets from one /24?
questions.explanation: The required block sizes are 128, 64, 32 and 16. They fit on descending boundaries and consume 240 addresses.

option_explanations.B: The required block sizes are 128, 64, 32 and 16. They fit on descending boundaries and consume 240 addresses.
option_explanations.D: The last block uses only 16 addresses, so the total remains below 256.

questions.question: A router advertises 10.20.8.0/21 to summarize its only networks, 10.20.8.0/24 through 10.20.11.0/24. Which extra range is covered?
questions.explanation: The /21 covers third octets 8–15, even though only 8–11 are present.

option_explanations.A: Those addresses belong to the component networks being summarized.
option_explanations.D: The /21 covers third octets 8–15, even though only 8–11 are present.

questions.question: Which pair covers exactly 203.0.113.0–203.0.113.191 using two aligned prefixes?
questions.explanation: The lower 128 addresses fit one /25 and the next 64 fit the aligned /26 starting at .128.

option_explanations.A: A /24 includes .192–.255 and already contains the proposed /26.
option_explanations.D: The lower 128 addresses fit one /25 and the next 64 fit the aligned /26 starting at .128.
